name: Ivan Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential; tell me both what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead a team at a tech company that makes appointment and stock software for repair shops. I read overnight fault reports, write code, review other people's changes, and call shop owners when a screen doesn't match what happened at the counter. I use AI coding tools every day, especially to try several fixes quickly. I have a master's degree, but the best part of the job is hearing that a mechanic found the right part on time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the rest of your life like around that job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone, earn ordinary senior-developer pay, and have saved roughly three months of expenses. My mother lives nearby, and I help her with errands on Sundays; she's not paying my bills. A few other software firms hire locally. I take risks on tools, but I won't put my rent or my mother's needs behind a business idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team our AI helper can draft code and tests, but the shop owner still decides if the stock count is right. We can use the saved hour to fix the old error list. I wouldn't sell a revolution to a mechanic waiting for a part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job feels secure enough, and three months saved gives me some space. I like being paid for judgment as well as typing. I would still ask whether our company is winning shops, because a bad product can sink a team without any new AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading releases and using AI on routine code, with a person checking each stock calculation. Starting this week I'd ask the sales lead for renewal numbers each month. In the first year I'd keep my regular savings transfer and put the freed hour into clearing known stock errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. My pay covers rent and the work still needs people who know repair shops. A missed renewal would concern me, but I don't expect one now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which known error would get that extra hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The system sometimes lists a returned alternator as new stock. I'd sit with a shop owner to trace the return before changing the code. A tidy screen can hide a very untidy shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for renewal numbers if you feel secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like a business to show its numbers. That's how I decide where to spend my work time, not a sign that I'm packing a box. There are a few local firms if I ever need to look.

say: I'd use **AI drafts** on routine code while people check repair-shop stock counts.
I'd spend the **saved hour** fixing known errors instead of promising a revolution.
think: I feel my **job and rent** are secure enough with three months saved.
I know **customer renewals** matter more to our present stability than minor AI gains.
do: Keep **leading releases** and checking stock calculations with shop owners.
Continue my **regular savings transfer** and ask sales for monthly customer renewal figures.
feel: **Calm** about income and work, with ordinary attention to whether shops renew.
S0.quote: A tidy screen can hide a very untidy shelf.
fieldNote: He uses AI daily but ties a **stock count** to what a mechanic sees on the shelf.
Typical pay and **three months saved** make this modest scenario feel manageable.
His renewal question reflects a **business habit**, not an expectation of imminent job loss.

steps.text: Keep leading software releases and checking stock counts with repair shops
Continue a regular monthly transfer into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues we should test AI on booking calls and code before competitors do. I'd invite two shop owners to judge whether the answers are useful. I would also ask the company to train apprentices on real counter problems, not only on prompting a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Faster code could mean fewer developers here, including a lead. I might be the one who runs the new system, but I can't assume that pays the same salary. Shops may also buy a cheaper service from someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd run a six-week trial on missed appointments and wrong stock orders, logging each mistake. I'd learn the new AI booking tool by building and checking a real shop workflow with its owner. If paid hours fall in the first year, I'd cut new gadget purchases and apply to local firms that still need customer-facing developers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and curious. I can move fast when a tool is useful, but I can't make a salary from curiosity alone. The rent comes out every month whether the trial works or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a shop owner test first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner of North Street Repairs to try booking a customer who changes the date twice. If AI loses the second change, we haven't saved the shop anything. I'd write down the result in front of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep an apprentice involved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the apprentice sit beside the shop owner for one afternoon, then explain the failed booking to our team. The owner knows the counter better than any screen. That meeting is worth more than another polished demo.

say: I'd test **AI bookings** with shop owners before claiming the service is better.
I'd keep **apprentices** learning real counter problems alongside the new tools.
think: I could lose **paid hours** if faster code reduces our team's size.
I cannot assume running the **new system** would preserve my senior salary.
do: Run a **six-week trial** on missed appointments and wrong orders this month.
Learn the **AI booking tool** by building a checked workflow with a shop owner.
Cut **gadget spending** and apply to local customer-facing developer roles if hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about pay, while curious enough to test the new tool quickly.
S1.quote: I can't make a salary from curiosity alone.
fieldNote: He seeks a **shop-owner trial** before wider use, despite being an eager daily AI user.
He wants apprentices to learn from **counter mistakes**, consistent with his practical view of training.
Spending cuts and local applications depend on **reduced paid hours**.

steps.text: Learn the new AI booking tool through a six-week shop-owner trial
Stop buying new gadgets if paid developer hours fall
Apply to nearby customer-facing developer jobs if paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that full thinking AI by 2028 could do our coding and customer replies before shop-floor robots arrive around 2031. A mechanic's hands won't save my screen job. I'd ask our boss for the staffing plan and speak plainly to apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of my income could disappear. Three months saved buys time, but not a whole new livelihood, and I won't ask my mother to cover rent. I can try to sell a service to shops, but a desperate sales pitch is not a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'd cancel the new laptop purchase and keep that money in emergency savings and ask two shop owners what problems would still be worth paying a person to solve. I'd request a reference from my boss and price short paid visits to fix messy stock records. In the first year after 2028, if my developer post ends, I'd take a paid shop systems job where one exists while testing those visits; I would only pay for tools from money left after rent and three months of essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can sketch three possible paths before breakfast, but I cannot guarantee even one pays by 2028. My mother's errands would still need doing if I lost this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mother my software wage may end and that I have three months of expenses saved. I'd ask her to let me keep Sunday errands practical, without pretending I can finance a new business overnight. She'd rather hear a plan than brave talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a paid shop visit worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One owner paying for a two-hour stock cleanup would prove more than ten compliments. I'd record the hours, travel cost and fee. If the fee doesn't cover those, I'd stop offering it.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches our code and replies before 2031 shop-floor robots.
I'd ask my boss for a **staffing plan** and tell apprentices the risk plainly.
think: I expect a **large income loss** and know three months saved cannot fund a new livelihood.
I won't rely on **my mother** to pay my rent or a business experiment.
do: Cancel the **new laptop purchase**, keep the money in emergency savings, and request a reference tomorrow.
Ask **two shop owners** about paid problems and price short stock-cleanup visits.
Take a **paid shop systems job** if laid off and one exists; buy tools only beyond rent and three months of essentials.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely income loss, despite several ideas and a three-month buffer.
S2.quote: A mechanic's hands won't save my screen job.
fieldNote: He understands the **2028 thinking shock** reaches him before robots reach repair shops around 2031.
His three-month **essentials buffer** is a floor, not seed money for a speculative business.
Stock-cleanup visits must **cover costs**; any shop-systems move requires a real paid opening.

steps.text: Cancel the new laptop purchase and keep that money in emergency savings
Offer stock cleanups if fees cover costs; buy tools only beyond rent and three months' essentials
Take a paid shop systems job if laid off and a vacancy exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company five years is enough to test services with shops and train people on their real needs. Full thinking AI in 2031 still threatens our code before robots arrive around 2034. I'd ask for a yearly report on roles, not just a speech about innovation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might build a small service that fixes inventory records for repair shops, but AI could make that cheap too. The useful question is whether owners pay me to handle the awkward handoff between software and shelves. I won't assume a friendly owner is a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I'd ask three shop owners to show me their worst stock mismatch and take a short evening course on small-business accounts, paid from my monthly learning budget without touching rent savings. I'd offer a paid trial to one shop while keeping my developer wage. In the first year after 2031, if two shops pay recurring fees covering the service costs, I'd add Saturday visits; if developer hours fall before that, I'd apply to local software firms rather than quit for an unproven offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years lets me test the numbers. I like building something of my own and I still need a wage. Both things can be true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the gap between a trial and a real second income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two shops paying each month, after travel and supplies, would make me call it income. One trial fee is evidence, not a living. I'd write the costs down where I can see them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why take an accounts course if you already have a master's degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My degree taught me software, not whether a small service is earning money. I want to know how to read costs before charging a neighbour. I can pay the course fee from my learning budget, but not the rent account.

say: I'd press for a **yearly role report** and paid tests of shop services before 2031.
I'd remind colleagues that **2034 robots** come after thinking AI changes software work.
think: I might earn from **inventory fixes**, but AI could cheapen that service too.
I need **paying owners**, since a friendly shop owner is not automatically a customer.
do: Take an **evening accounts course** from my learning budget without touching rent savings.
Offer **one paid trial** while keeping the developer wage, then add visits only after two shops pay recurring cost-covering fees.
Apply to **local software firms** if developer hours fall before shop fees cover costs.
feel: **Anxious** about income, with five years to test a side service and keep wages.
S3.quote: One trial fee is evidence, not a living.
fieldNote: He distinguishes a **paid trial** from recurring income after travel and supplies.
The accounts course uses a **separate learning budget**, preserving rent savings.
He keeps the developer wage and adds **Saturday visits** only after two shops pay recurring fees.

steps.text: Take an evening small-business accounts course using a separate learning budget
Offer one paid stock-cleanup trial while keeping the developer wage
Add Saturday stock visits only after two shops pay recurring fees covering costs
Apply to local software firms if developer hours fall before shop fees cover costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell apprentices a decade gives them time to learn the customer's trade as well as software. I'd build a service with repair shops now and let real invoices tell me if it works. Thinking AI in 2036 could still replace our code before robots reach workshops around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have several years of paid shop relationships and a deeper cash buffer by then. I might also be wrong about what shops need, so I want small tests rather than a grand launch. I don't want my mother or my future family to carry the cost of my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my salary and set aside a fixed monthly amount for savings before any product spending. I'd work with one repair shop each quarter, charging for stock cleanup and recording whether the fee covers travel and hours. In the first year after 2036, if development income falls and the shop service has paid recurring customers covering basic bills for six months, I'd expand it; otherwise I'd apply for paid shop systems roles where vacancies exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not sleepless. Three months saved and an ordinary salary make today stable, and ten years is time to learn. I still wouldn't call a future customer certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you stop doing if the service loses money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop Saturday visits after two quarters of fees below costs and keep the developer job. I can tell a neighbour a service isn't working without making a family debt out of it. Pride costs more when you hide the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you see your mother's part in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother can tell me which shops she trusts, but I won't ask her for start-up money. I help with errands, and I'd keep those Sundays free. Family support goes both ways without turning into an invoice.

say: I'd urge apprentices to learn **repair-shop work** as well as software across the decade.
I'd let **paid invoices** judge a small service before betting on a launch.
think: I could build **customers and savings** before 2036, though the service might fail.
I won't make **my mother** or a future family carry the cost of my pride.
do: Keep my **developer salary** and save a fixed amount before product spending.
Charge **one shop each quarter** for stock cleanup and stop visits after two losing quarters.
Expand after 2036 only with **six months** of bill-covering revenue if developer income falls; otherwise seek paid shop systems vacancies.
feel: **Uneasy** about later income, while current salary and savings provide security.
S4.quote: Pride costs more when you hide the numbers.
fieldNote: His traditional family view appears in a firm **no-family-debt rule** and Sunday time with his mother.
He keeps the **salary first** and tests shop work against invoices each quarter.
Expansion requires **six months** of bill-covering revenue; otherwise a move needs a paid vacancy.

steps.text: Transfer a fixed amount monthly into savings before product spending
Charge quarterly stock visits; expand only after six months of bill-covering revenue and falling developer income
Apply for paid shop systems vacancies if developer income falls and service revenue cannot cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My screen work would face it before the workshop robots arrive, and three months saved won't last through a long job search. Clear notice, paid training with a repair shop, and a list of actual local vacancies would help me move fast without gambling rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether shop owners trust the new system when a part goes missing. I can write brilliant code and still lose a mechanic's trust with one wrong stock count. I'd want the owner to be able to question and correct the record.

headlineQuote: I can write brilliant code and still lose a mechanic's trust with one wrong stock count.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old senior developer** with a master's degree, leading software work for repair shops.
He earns **typical pay**, lives alone and has three months saved, with some nearby software employers and a mother he helps.
A **daily AI user**, he measures tools against the shop floor and trains apprentices through real customer problems.
The **2028 shock** alarms him because coding income could fall before a side service earns reliable money.
Longer timelines let him test **paid stock services** while protecting rent and his developer wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his screen-based wage before three months saved supports a long search.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice**, paid repair-shop training and a list of actual local vacancies would help him.
